📊 About This Simulation

Physics: The particle is prepared in a Gaussian wavefunction ψ(x). Measurement outcomes follow the Born rule, so the position probability density is |ψ(x)|². Repeated measurements on identically prepared states reproduce the theoretical distribution.

Simulation visuals: The top plot shows the theoretical wavefunction view (probability, real part, imaginary part, or both real/imaginary). The bottom plot shows measured outcomes as a normalized histogram, overlaid with the theoretical |ψ(x)|² curve for comparison.

Controls: Run single-shot or batch measurements, enable auto-measurement and set its rate, adjust animation speed, switch view mode, and reset measurements. The Statistics panel reports total count, mean position, measured standard deviation, theoretical σ, and convergence.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The prepared state

Here’s the set-up. Before every measurement, the particle is prepared in the same Gaussian state ψ(x), of width σ. The upper plot draws that state — either its probability density |ψ(x)|² or its real and imaginary parts. The lower plot collects the positions your measurements actually return, as a normalized histogram against the theoretical |ψ(x)|².

2 · Identical preparations

Let’s start with the classical view. Each measurement acts on a freshly prepared copy of the same state. What do you think classical physics would predict for the record of a hundred position measurements?

3 · A wave that dips below zero

Let’s look at the wave itself. The upper plot now draws Re(ψ), which swings above and below the axis as the phase turns. At an instant when the whole curve lies below the axis, where do you think the particle is most likely to be found?

4 · A thousand more

Time for more data. About a hundred measurements now sit on the lower plot, and we’re about to add a thousand more. What do you think happens to the height of the central bars?

5 · While the phase turns

One last experiment. The upper plot now shows Re(ψ) and Im(ψ) together, with the phase turning quickly, and the histogram has been cleared. What do you think the next thousand measurements will build?

The Physics

Wavefunctions and |ψ|² · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

In quantum mechanics the wavefunction ψ(x) is used to predict the results of position measurements. This sim prepares one state and measures its position again and again, so you can compare the record of results with the curve that predicts it.

What you'll learn

  • How a wavefunction is turned into probabilities (the Born rule).
  • How Re ψ, Im ψ and |ψ|² are related, and which of them a position measurement depends on.
  • How the height of the histogram bars depends on how many results you have.
  • How the measured mean and spread depend on the number of measurements N.
Top: the prepared state. Bottom: the record that each measurement adds one position to.

What's on screen

  • Upper plot, "Theoretical Function": the prepared state. |ψ(x)|² is violet, Re ψ is blue and Im ψ is pink. Position x is marked in units of σ, from −4σ to +4σ.
  • Lower plot, "Measurement Results": blue bars are the record, a pink dashed curve is the theoretical |ψ|², and an amber flash marks the newest result.
  • Statistics panel: the number of measurements, their mean and standard deviation, σ = 1.00, and a Convergence bar.
See itClear the record and take 100 position measurements. Watch for: the Total counting up to 100 while blue bars appear in the lower plot.

03

One state, many outcomes

The sim prepares a Gaussian state with width σ and measures its position:

The prepared state and its probability density. The factor e−iωt is a phase; section 04 returns to it.

The Born rule turns ψ into probabilities. |ψ(x)|² is a probability density: its integral over an interval is the probability of a result in that interval.

The Born rule, and normalisation: the total probability is 1.
  • One measurement returns one number x. Prepare the same state again and the sim returns a different x. The Born rule predicts frequencies: about 68% of results fall within ±1σ, and about 95% within ±2σ.
  • ψ has units of 1/√length, so |ψ|² is probability per length. With σ = 1 the peak is 1/√(2π) = 0.399, the top tick on the lower plot.
See itPrepare the same state five times, measuring once each time. Watch for: five different values of Mean Position (with one result, the mean is that result).
04

Re ψ and Im ψ combine into |ψ|²

ψ is a complex number at each x. The sim writes it as a fixed envelope A(x) ≥ 0 times a phase that turns with time, so its two parts swing between +A and −A:

  • Re ψ (blue) and Im ψ (pink) go negative for part of each turn. A probability density cannot, and it does not: |ψ|² = (Re ψ)² + (Im ψ)², and squaring removes the sign.
  • The dashed outline in the Re and Im views is ±A(x). It never moves. Those views are scaled so that the peak of A is 1 (axis "Amplitude"), unlike the |ψ|² view, whose axis shows density up to 0.399.
See itShow Re ψ, slow the phase to 0.2×, clear the record and take 1000 measurements. Watch for: the blue Re ψ dipping below the axis (within about 4 s) while the bars below build a hump.
05

Why the bars are densities, not counts

The lower plot has 50 bins of width Δ = 0.16σ across −4σ to +4σ. Each bar is the fraction of results in its bin, divided by Δ:

Bar height hk from the count ck in bin k.
  • Bar area = fraction of results in that bin, so the bars always add up to area 1, whatever N is. Extra data does not raise the bars; it makes them settle onto the dashed curve, which is drawn on the same scale.
  • A result beyond ±4σ (about 1 in 16,000) is counted in the statistics but has no bar.

With fewer than about 15 results, a single count is already taller than the plot allows, so its bar is drawn cut off at the top.

See itRecord 100 results, then 1000 more. Watch for: the bars settling onto the pink dashed curve rather than rising above it.
06

How fast the record converges

The Statistics panel estimates two properties of the state: the mean position (0) and the spread (σ = 1). Both estimates scatter around the true value by an amount that shrinks as N grows:

Typical scatter of the mean and of the measured standard deviation s.
per click

This control moves the sim's Measurements per click too.

  • The error falls as 1/√N: halving it costs four times the data, and ten times the data buys about three times the accuracy.
  • The Convergence bar is 100(1 − |s − σ|/σ) percent, so it measures only the spread, not the mean.
See itMeasure 10 results, then 100 more, then 1000 more. Watch for: the Measured Std Dev, rough at N = 10, sitting close to 1.00 by N = 1110.
07

A turning phase changes no probabilities

In this sim the phase factor e−iωt is the same at every x, so it cancels when you form |ψ|²:

  • Only the split between Re ψ and Im ψ changes with time (one full turn takes about 1 s at 1.0×). Every measurable density, and so every histogram, stays the same.
  • The distribution does not drift: this state has ⟨p⟩ = 0. A drifting distribution needs a phase that varies with x, such as eikx.

Not modelled: the width stays σ for ever. That is right for a stationary state such as the ground state of a harmonic oscillator, but a free packet released from rest would spread.

See itShow Re ψ and Im ψ at 4× speed, clear the record and take 1000 measurements. Watch for: Re ψ and Im ψ trading places inside the fixed dashed outline while the bars below build one hump.
08

Where it matters

  • Single-electron interference. In 1989 Tonomura and colleagues sent electrons one at a time through an electron biprism. Each arrived as a single dot, and the interference fringes showed up only after tens of thousands of dots had accumulated.
  • Scanning-tunnelling images. Electrons held inside a ring of atoms on a metal surface (a "quantum corral") show up as standing-wave rings. The image brightness follows the local density of states, built from |ψ|² of the electron states.
  • Orbital pictures. Chemistry textbooks draw an orbital as a surface of constant |ψ|², commonly chosen to enclose 90% of the probability.
Go deeper: the price of a narrow state

This Gaussian has the smallest possible product of position and momentum spreads, ΔxΔp = ħ/2. The sim does not show momentum, but the relation is why a narrow state is hard to keep still:

It is also the ground state of a harmonic oscillator when σ² = ħ/(2mω₀). Its phase then turns at ω = ω₀/2, which is E₀/ħ.

09

Summary

In one line. |ψ(x)|² is the probability density for position measurements: each measurement gives one value, and only the frequencies are predicted, ever more sharply as N grows.

Key points

  • P(a ≤ x ≤ b) = ∫|ψ|² dx over [a, b], and the total area is 1.
  • Re ψ and Im ψ can be negative; |ψ|² = (Re ψ)² + (Im ψ)² cannot.
  • The bars are densities, count ÷ (N · 0.16σ), so more data sharpens them without raising them.
  • The scatter of the mean and of the spread both shrink as 1/√N.

Common mix-ups

  • "Where Re ψ is negative, the probability is negative." The probability density is |ψ|², which is never negative.
  • "More measurements make the bars taller." The bars settle onto the curve, and the total area stays 1.
  • "The turning phase makes the distribution move." One phase that is the same at every x cancels out of |ψ|².

Things to try on your own

  • Set Measurements per click to 10, press Reset, then Measure, and note the Measured Std Dev. Repeat five times and compare the scatter with the typical 0.24 for N = 10.
  • Choose Re ψ & Im ψ at 0.2× and time one full turn with a stopwatch (about 5 s). Then try 4.0×.
  • Switch Auto Measure on at 100/s and note the Total at which you can no longer see the bars differ from the dashed curve.
